extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, parents and educators, writers and literary critics (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Early-18th-century essays giving prescriptive advice on social conduct (beauty, marriage, fashion), education policy, and standards for evaluating epic poetry and characterisation. Includes concrete examples and prescriptions for public practice (schools, marriage examination) and criteria for literary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin a new life by severing ties with past beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: When a woman has lost her beauty (e.g., to smallpox), she should begin a new life by burning or returning love-letters and severing reciprocal tokens tied to her former condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested practice: 'burn all her Love-Letters; ... send them back to those who writ them, with this honest Inscription, Articles of a Marriage Treaty broken off by the Small-Pox.' Example letter (Corinna→Amilcar) contrasts flattery vs sincere affection as test of constancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature outweighs beauty in attractiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Good-nature and an easy, cheerful behaviour supply what beauty cannot; they make a person truly agreeable and sustain affection when beauty is gone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit claim: 'Good-Nature will always supply the Absence of Beauty, but Beauty cannot long supply the Absence of Good-Nature.' Examples: the modest, attentive woman who accompanies a man in cares and joys; contrast with 'Beauties' who are impertinent and self-absorbed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unselfconsciousness as a key charm
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who does not perceive themself as an object of love often becomes the object of stronger affection than one outwardly knowing and cultivating their charms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: a lover admired a woman in a crowd who was the least remarkable for beauty—her surprise at being looked at revealed she did not regard herself as an object of desire, which explained her charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise the anti-patterns of conventional 'beauties'
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspicuous beauties often show impatience for admiration, self-reflection on their merit, and a 'precious behaviour' that makes them disagreeable as companions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: 'An apparent Desire of Admiration, a Reflection upon their own Merit, and a precious Behaviour ... are almost inseparable Accidents in Beauties.' Husbands of great Beauties will often find them disagreeable, i.e., beauty can produce daily irritations rather than durable affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt education to a child's natural genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should be tailored to a youth's natural temperament and talents; nothing can substitute for suitability of nature to a particular art or science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: Juan Huarte (Nothing but Nature can qualify a Man for Learning), Plato's method of questioning to 'help the birth' of knowledge, and the example of Marcus (Cicero's son) and Clavius (initially deemed hopeless until tried in geometry). Practical proposal: appoint state tryers/examiners to inspect a boy's genius and allot him suitable studies/professions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing all children into a uniform curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: It is mistaken to require boys of differing ages, temperaments and inclinations to study the same authors and perform the same tasks as if they all had identical capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'forty or fifty Boys of several Ages ... ranged together in the same Class' and forced to be 'Poets, Historians, and Orators alike.' The root cause: parents' refusal to accept differences and insistence their sons equal their neighbours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity and state schools should examine and distribute by talent
rubrics_metrics.description: In institutions (especially charity schools) directors should examine pupils to allocate them into proper classes and assign studies or apprenticeships according to aptitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guidance: well-examining parts, 'make a just Distribution of them into proper Classes and Divisions,' and allot professions, trades, handicrafts, or service as their genius qualifies them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match vocation to capacity; regulate professions by fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Public good requires preventing unfit persons from entering professions (e.g., clergy, law) for which they are unsuited; many who fail in one station might excel in another practical station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man running his head against a pulpit who might serve well at a plough-tail; an indifferent barrister who would have made a good waterman. Implication: state or institutional oversight should discourage misplacement of talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public selection and early allocation (Spartan model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A civic system that inspects youths early and assigns them to public companies based on observed talents avoids parental bias and builds effective civic/military discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spartan example: from age seven children listed into companies, performances observed by elders who set them at strife to discover talents, leading Sparta to military/civil supremacy. Implied prescription: an analogous regulated examination from childhood benefits the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine consent and motives before marriage (marriage-censor)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be an officer or censor who examines those about to marry to ensure consent is free and not coerced by parents or interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal: inspect whether parties are 'forced by Parents on one Side, or moved by Interest only on the other' to avoid matches that produce 'awkward Heirs' from half-love and constrained compliance. Parallel drawn to judicial examination before conveyance of a wife's estate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of fashion-driven domestic consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive pursuit of fashion in apparel and household furnishings is wasteful, harms domestic contentment, and can alienate spouses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter example: a husband complains his wife's constant refurnishing and insistence on fashionable dining leave him eating at a chop-house; fashion as an enforced stomach-upsetting requirement is a social ill to be reproved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency in epic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons introduced in a poem should display sentiments and behaviour perfectly suited to their respective characters; every circumstance in their speeches and actions should be justly adapted to who they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General principle stated: 'Every Circumstance in their Speeches and Actions is with great Justness and Delicacy adapted to the Persons who speak and act.' Examples: Satan's mock-majesty and daring; Moloch's fury; Belial's timorous and slothful nature; Mammon's covetousness; Beelzebub as moderator proposing action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit speeches and actions to rank and role
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's formal role (leader, moderator, instigator) should be reflected in how they open/close debates and the quality of their speech; e.g., Satan opens and closes the debate, Beelzebub moderates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Satan 'opening and closing the Debate' fits his superior greatness; Beelzebub 'acts as a kind of Moderator' proposing a measured alternative (search for a new world). This alignment reinforces plausibility and dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain previously established character traits across episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's depiction in one book must remain coherent with prior descriptions across subsequent books (e.g., Moloch's fierceness, Mammon's materialism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Moloch described in Book I as besmeared with blood and in Book II as the fiercest spirit; Mammon's speech is suitable to one obsessed with pomp and riches. Consistency yields 'agreeable Variety' when contrasted with other speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrast of thought and speech for variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternating or contrasting viewpoints among speakers (rash vs prudent, furious vs timorous) gives agreeable variety and movement to assemblies or debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Belial's timorous caution contrasted with other speakers produces variety; the contrast with preceding speech enhances the debate's interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy in descriptive episodes — avoid overextension
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes and descriptive digressions should be kept proportionate; a poet should not 'spin out' circumstantial description so long that it weakens the main fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise of Milton: 'This Episode of the fallen Spirits, and their Place of Habitation, comes in very happily to unbend the Mind of the Reader ... An ordinary Poet would ... have spun out so many Circumstances to a great Length, and by that means have weakned, instead of illustrated, the principal Fable.' Keep episodes tight and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful effect through concise, evocative lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A single, well-chosen line can convey more horror or splendor than extended detail; brevity in certain images increases their horror or force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a single line listing monstrous creations ('Gorgons, and Hydras, and Chimeras dire') gives a more horrid idea than a long description would. Use concentrated imagery where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allegory is effective but may be limited in epic context
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegorical pieces can be 'very finished' in themselves, but their suitability must be judged when they function as parts of a larger epic poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific note: the allegory of Sin and Death is 'a very finished Piece in its kind, when it is not considered as a Part of an Epic Poem' — implying caution: allegory should not impair epic unity or plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place thematic or prophetic material early to ground the poem's project
rubrics_metrics.description: Important thematic material (e.g., the project of a new world / creation of Man) may be mentioned early to prepare and justify the poem's central action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: Milton's earlier mention of a possible new world in Book I was 'just' because the subsequent poem turns on that project; such early foreshadowing or prophecy dignifies later developments and links acts of principal characters to the poem's central design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match diversions and amusements to characters' misapplied faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Depictions of leisure (races, feats of arms, music, entertainments) should be appropriate to characters who retain only misapplied strength and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's fallen angels engage in contests, feats of arms, and music celebrating their crimes — diversions 'every way suitable to Beings who had nothing left them but Strength and Knowledge misapplied.' Use such activities to underline character corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose sublime imagery for grand actions (rising, movement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublime effects in narrative — e.g., simultaneous rising of an assembly — should be rendered in powerful, sonorous images that evoke scale and awe (e.g., 'Their rising all at once was as the Sound / Of Thunder heard remote').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: use metaphors of natural force (thunder, tempest) and compact diction to convey majesty and vast movement in a few lines.
